title: A non-cubic space-filling modular robot
text:
When Johannes Kepler peered into the hexagonal cells of honeycombs he saw three rhombi at their base (Fig. A non-cubic space-filling modular robot A,B). Capping a cell with three more rhombi, Kepler sketched a rhombic dodecahedron. But the shape was already on his mind. Studying how snowflakes could be built from microscopic spheres of ice, Kepler made the following conjecture [1]: no packing of congruent spheres has density greater than that of the face-centered cubic packing (Fig. A non-cubic space-filling modular robot C), in which each sphere touches 12 others, and which fills just over 74% of space. When uniformly compressed, these spheres will deform into space-filling polyhedra with twelve faces: rhombic dodecahedra (Fig. A non-cubic space-filling modular robot D).

Since Kepler’s discovery of the shape in the early 17th century, rhombic dodecahedra have been found in crystals of viruses [3], proteins [4], carbohydrates [5], metals [6] and minerals [7]. These self-assembling crystalline structures have been of keen interest in several fields of engineering due to their exceptional optical, catalytic, electronic and magnetic properties [8,9], which suggests that space filling in general, and the dodecahedral morphology in particular, may also be useful for self-assembling modular robots [10].

Like crystals, modular robots can “grow” to form multicellular bodies by ceaselessly combining and separating unit cells. Such robots—if space-filling—could form gapless containers, pipes, mirrors, shields, submersibles, spaceships and extraterrestrial habitats on the fly. And by virtue of broader surface contacts between neighbors, space-filling robots could build much more stable and energetically favorable superstructures than non-space-filling robots [11].

Many unit shapes have been explored in robotics: triangles [12], hexagons [13], spheres [14], cubes [15], cuboids [16], cylinders [17] semi-cylinders [18] and cylindroids [19]. But only two of these shapes were built to attach in 3D space (spheres and cubes), and only one was capable of filling it: cubes.

The cube is a parallelohedron [20]: a congruent polyhedron that can be translated to completely fill space, without rotations. In other words, space can be partitioned into a regular lattice by cubes. In addition to the cube, which has square faces, there are just four other parallelohedra: the rhombic dodecahedron (rhombic faces), the hexagonal prism (hexagonal and cubic faces), the elongated dodecahedron (rhombic and octagonal faces), and the truncated octahedron (cubic, rhombic, and hexagonal faces). The cube and the rhombic dodecahedron are the simplest parallelohedra. Their isometric faces (all squares or all rhombi) allow two cells to connect on all sides, which simplifies the assembly and reconfiguration of multicellular bodies.

There is an infinitude of other polyhedra that, alone or in combination with additional polyhedra, via translations, rotations or reflections, along periodic or aperiodic tilings, can fill space without any gaps. Out of all of these possible shapes, only the cube has been taken seriously in robotics. Indeed, the vast majority of modular robots built to date have been either cubes or cuboids [21].

Rhombic dodecahedra have an advantage kinematically over cubes that was first noted by [22]: Cubes require two kinds of inherently difficult rolling/rotational motions (90 \degree and 180 \degree; Fig. 2 A and B) to move about each other, and can incur considerable sliding friction against any cubes perpendicular to the axis of rotation. Rhombic dodecahedra, in contrast, require only a single simple rotational movement (120°; Fig. 2 C), and eliminate the need for any part of the cells to slide against each other, while preserving the good property of cubes: Once two opposing faces of two cells are aligned and connected, all rotations about one of the four shared edges will result in another pair of aligned faces.

After neatly illustrating this, [22] went on to show how to coordinate the self-assembly of virtual rhombic dodecahedra toward target shapes, but, until now, no such robots have been created. Thus here we design and deploy the first rhombic dodecahedra robots. While they cannot yet assemble themselves, their physicality helps us envisage a future in which they do.
